title: Trendelenburg Sign | Hip Abductor Weakness Assessment | Hip OA
purpose: Detect hip abductor weakness (gluteus medius and minimus) of the stance leg, as often seen in hip osteoarthritis; evaluated as a test for hip OA.
structure: Gluteus medius and minimus of the stance leg; pelvis/iliac crest height.
procedure: Patient standing (may hold the wall for balance) and flexes one hip to 90°. The examiner compares the height of both iliac crests; normally the side of the flexed hip is higher.
positive: The iliac crest on the flexed-hip side drops below the stance side, or the patient compensates by leaning the trunk toward the stance leg, indicating weak abductors of the stance leg. Some authors define positive as a femoral (pelvis-on-femur) angle ≤ 83° on the stance leg held for 30 s.
notes: Authors conclude the test is not useful for identifying early hip OA. Other hip OA tests on the page: Patrick's/FABER, Cluster of Sutlive, signs & symptoms of hip OA.

title: Single Leg Stance Test | Gluteal Tendinopathy (GTPS)
purpose: Diagnose gluteal tendinopathy (under the umbrella term greater trochanteric pain syndrome, GTPS) in patients with lateral hip pain.
structure: Gluteus medius/minimus tendons at the greater trochanter.
procedure: Patient stands beside a wall with the affected leg furthest from the wall, touching the wall with one finger of the unaffected side at shoulder height. The patient lifts the unaffected foot by flexing the knee to 90° while keeping that hip neutral, and holds for up to 30 seconds.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's lateral hip pain at the greater trochanter of at least 2/10 on the NPRS within 30 seconds.

accuracy.source: Grimaldi et al. (cited as 2016 in text, reference list says 2017, BJSM); Lequesne et al. 2008

notes: Grimaldi's setting (symptomatic patients only) mirrors clinical practice better: a positive test practically rules the condition in, a negative test cannot exclude it; page rates it strong clinical value for inclusion. Other GTPS tests: resisted external derotation, greater trochanter palpation, FADER/FADER-R, ADD/ADD-R (modified Ober's).

title: Piriformis Test | Piriformis Syndrome or Piriformis Tightness Assessment
purpose: Assess piriformis tightness / piriformis syndrome, now termed deep gluteal syndrome (DGS).
structure: Piriformis and the sciatic nerve in the subgluteal space. In about 15% of people the sciatic nerve passes through the piriformis. DGS = buttock pain from non-discogenic sciatic nerve entrapment; possible culprits also include fibrous/vascular bands, gluteal and hamstring muscles, the gemelli-obturator internus complex, vascular abnormalities and space-occupying lesions.
procedure: Patient side-lying at the edge of the table. Bring the upper leg to 60° hip flexion with the knee flexed, lower leg fully extended. Fixate the pelvis with one hand and apply downward pressure at the knee with the other.
positive: Pain in the buttock area or pain radiating down the back of the leg.
notes: Typical DGS symptoms on the page: sciatica-like unilateral buttock/hip pain and retro-trochanteric tenderness, worse with hip rotation in flexion plus knee extension, intolerance of sitting > 20-30 min, limping, sensory disturbance, night pain improving by day. Other DGS tests: HCLK maneuver, Pace, Freiberg, FAIR, Beatty, seated piriformis stretch, active piriformis. No references listed.

title: Active Piriformis Test | Piriformis Syndrome | Deep Gluteal Syndrome of the Hip
purpose: Diagnose sciatic nerve entrapment in the gluteal region (deep gluteal syndrome, DGS).
structure: Piriformis (S2-S4 to greater trochanter) and sciatic nerve in the subgluteal space.
procedure: Exclude lumbar spine and SIJ pathology first. Patient side-lying on the unaffected side, flexes the upper knee and places the foot on the table. The examiner palpates the piriformis and resists at the flexed knee while the patient drives the heel into the table, producing active hip abduction and external rotation.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar gluteal pain and/or paraesthesia radiating into the posterior lower extremity.

accuracy.source: Martin et al. (cited as 2013 in text; reference list says 2014, KSSTA), endoscopically confirmed entrapment

notes: Only study so far; page rates moderate clinical value for both ruling in and out. Other DGS tests: Freiberg, FAIR, seated piriformis stretch, HCLK, piriformis test, Beatty, Pace.

title: Seated Piriformis Stretch Test | Piriformis Syndrome | Deep Gluteal Syndrome Hip
purpose: Diagnose sciatic nerve entrapment in the gluteal region (deep gluteal syndrome) by lengthening the deep hip rotators and tensioning the sciatic nerve.
structure: Deep external rotators of the hip (piriformis) and sciatic nerve at the sciatic notch.
procedure: Exclude lumbar spine and SIJ pathology first. Patient sits over the edge of the table with the hip at about 90° flexion and the knee extended. While palpating the sciatic notch, the examiner adducts and internally rotates the limb.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar gluteal pain and/or paraesthesia radiating into the posterior lower extremity.

accuracy.source: Martin et al. (cited as 2013 in text; reference list says 2014, KSSTA), endoscopically confirmed entrapment

notes: Only study so far; page rates moderate clinical value for confirming the condition. Other DGS tests: HCLK, Pace, Freiberg, FAIR, piriformis test, Beatty, active piriformis.

title: FAIR Test | Piriformis Syndrome | Deep Gluteal Syndrome of the Hip
purpose: Provoke sciatic nerve compression by the piriformis (Flexion-Adduction-Internal Rotation) in suspected deep gluteal syndrome.
structure: Piriformis and sciatic nerve in the subgluteal space.
procedure: Exclude lumbar spine and SIJ pathology first. Patient lies on the unaffected side with the upper hip flexed to 90°, maximally adducted, and the upper knee flexed to 90°. Keeping both acetabula vertical, the examiner applies upward and lateral pressure to the shin while passively internally rotating the hip to 45° or as far as tolerated.
positive: Pain at the intersection of the sciatic nerve and the piriformis.

accuracy.source: Fishman et al. 2002, against H-reflex delay of 3 SD above normal

notes: H-reflex is sensitive but not specific and not an accurate gold standard; no other studies, so the page rates clinical value questionable. Other DGS tests: Freiberg, Pace, seated piriformis stretch, HCLK, piriformis test, Beatty, active piriformis.

title: Freiberg Sign | Piriformis Syndrome | Deep Gluteal Syndrome Hip
purpose: Provoke sciatic nerve compression by stretching an irritated piriformis in suspected deep gluteal syndrome.
procedure: Exclude lumbar spine and SIJ pathology first. Patient supine. The examiner forcefully internally rotates the extended thigh of the affected leg.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar gluteal pain and/or paraesthesia radiating into the posterior lower extremity.

accuracy.source: n/a: page states no diagnostic studies exist (Freiberg 1937; Kirschner 2009)

notes: Clinical value rated questionable. Other DGS tests: HCLK, Pace, seated piriformis stretch, FAIR, piriformis test, Beatty, active piriformis.

title: Pace Maneuver | Piriformis Syndrome | Deep Gluteal Syndrome of the Hip
purpose: Provocation test for deep gluteal syndrome / piriformis syndrome.
procedure: SOURCE ISSUE: the page's execution paragraph is identical to the FAIR test page ('as shown in the study of Fishman': side-lying on the unaffected side, upper hip 90° flexion, maximal adduction, knee 90°, upward/lateral pressure on the shin with internal rotation to 45°). This appears to be a copy-paste error on physiotutors.com; the original Pace & Nagle (1976) maneuver is not described in the page text. Refer to the video for the actual execution.
positive: Per the page text: pain at the intersection of the sciatic nerve and the piriformis (same wording as the FAIR page).

accuracy.source: n/a: page states no diagnostic studies exist (Pace & Nagle 1976; Kirschner 2009)

notes: Clinical value rated questionable. Exclude lumbar spine and SIJ pathology first. Other DGS tests: Freiberg, FAIR, seated piriformis stretch, HCLK, piriformis test, Beatty, active piriformis.

title: Beatty Maneuver | Piriformis Syndrome | Deep Gluteal Syndrome Hip
purpose: Simple provocation maneuver for piriformis syndrome / deep gluteal syndrome.
procedure: Exclude lumbar spine and SIJ pathology first. Patient lies on the unaffected side with hips and knees flexed, then actively abducts the upper thigh so that it lifts off the table.
positive: Deep buttock pain on the affected (upper) side. Back pain instead is described in patients with lumbar disc disease.

accuracy.source: n/a: page states no diagnostic studies exist (Beatty 1994; Kirschner 2009)

notes: Clinical value rated questionable. Other DGS tests: HCLK, Pace, Freiberg, FAIR, piriformis test, seated piriformis stretch, active piriformis.
